heading: Reading the Serrow Cairns: Registers, Cant and the Pell Stone
takeaway: A Serrow cairn carries two independent registers of meaning — a fixed builder's message encoded in course cant (dorran) and a rolling record of recent conditions carried only by the pell stone (lisk) — and most misreadings come from collapsing that distinction or from mistaking an incidental feature (lean, a low concord score, a stale or reset stone) for a meaningful signal in one register or the other.

ideas.label: dorran sense: the builder's fixed message, encoded in course cant, unchanged until rebuilding
ideas.anchor: The dorran sense is whatever the builder put into the arrangement of the courses

misconceptions.claim: the builder's message can drift over time just like trail conditions do
misconceptions.provenance: misreads 'does not change unless the cairn is rebuilt' as a general tendency rather than an absolute

misconceptions.claim: the dorran sense is carried by the pell stone, same as the lisk sense
misconceptions.provenance: misreads 'a small loose stone rests on the crown' as the general carrier of meaning, not realizing dorran lives in the courses

misconceptions.claim: Brannagh's objection shows the dorran sense isn't really fixed either, since the builder's original choices were somewhat arbitrary
misconceptions.provenance: misreads Brannagh's point about the lisk sense's seed position as if it were about the dorran sense instead

ideas.label: lisk sense: a rolling record of recent conditions, carried by the pell stone alone
ideas.anchor: The lisk sense is carried by the pell stone alone

misconceptions.claim: a physical marker's meaning is fixed once built, so the pell stone must just be decoration
misconceptions.provenance: misreads 'a small loose stone rests on the crown; it is called the pell stone' as non-functional ornament

misconceptions.claim: the lisk sense records where the route goes, and it is the builder who updates it on revisits
misconceptions.provenance: reverses which sense is fixed and which is dynamic, and swaps which party (builder vs. passer) updates it

misconceptions.claim: the lisk sense is entirely independent of the builder
misconceptions.provenance: misreads Brannagh's objection ('the lisk sense is not independent of the builder... sets the pell stone's first position') as having been refuted, when surveyors 'nonetheless still record the two registers separately'

ideas.label: Hessle cairns (dorran only) vs Garth cairns (lisk only) as single-register edge cases
ideas.anchor: A Hessle cairn has canted body courses but no pell stone
ideas.reason: corollary of SC-1/SC-2 naming the two single-register edge cases; folds naturally as a conflation distractor in the dorran/lisk question rather than supporting an independent hold

ideas.label: lean: whole-cairn tilt from frost heave, meaningless
ideas.anchor: Lean is the tilt of the cairn as a whole away from the vertical

misconceptions.claim: any irregularity in a marker must be meaningful
misconceptions.provenance: misreads the existence of measurable lean as itself significant, contradicted by 'Lean... carries no meaning'

misconceptions.claim: lean is the builder's deliberate offset of the whole cairn
misconceptions.provenance: conflates lean with cant rather than treating lean as an accidental artifact of frost heave under the footing

misconceptions.claim: lean is caused by deliberate builder choice or by a heavy pell stone
misconceptions.provenance: reverses the stated cause: lean 'is almost always produced by frost heave under the footing'

ideas.label: cant: deliberate, course-relative offset that points the route's turn
ideas.anchor: Cant is the deliberate offset of a single course, a body course or the crown

misconceptions.claim: cant is judged against true vertical, the same way lean is
misconceptions.provenance: misreads 'relative to the course beneath it' as if cant were measured against the vertical like lean

misconceptions.claim: a subtle offset in a course must be a construction flaw, not a signal
misconceptions.provenance: pre-chapter prior contradicted by cant being the builder's deliberate direction-pointer

misconceptions.claim: an offset outside 'about a finger's width' isn't real cant at all
misconceptions.provenance: misapplies the reliability detail about how well strangers read cant into a claim about what counts as cant

ideas.label: lean misleads experienced readers more than it misleads strangers
ideas.anchor: Lean misleads experienced readers more often than it misleads strangers

misconceptions.claim: expertise should reduce misreading error across the board
misconceptions.provenance: pre-chapter prior contradicted directly by the stated finding that lean misleads experienced readers more

misconceptions.claim: locals are fooled by lean because they cannot perceive cant at all
misconceptions.provenance: misreads the actual mechanism, that locals 'judge cant by eye against the vertical' (silhouette) rather than course against course

misconceptions.claim: since strangers misroute more often overall, they must also be more often misled by lean specifically
misconceptions.provenance: imports the general Sources-of-error finding (strangers misroute ~19% vs locals ~4%) into this specific case, where the relation is reversed

ideas.label: concord index counting mechanics: footing excluded, pairs with an uncanted course excluded
ideas.anchor: The footing is excluded, since it follows the slope of the ground and has no cant of its own
ideas.reason: computational bookkeeping rule; needed to compute SC-8/SC-9 and the worked example but is a procedural detail (fact to have), not a hold

ideas.label: Marhaug's concord index includes the crown as the uppermost course
ideas.anchor: In Marhaug's version the crown is included as the uppermost course

misconceptions.claim: Marhaug's crown-included version is still the version in active use
misconceptions.provenance: misreads the historical framing and conflates the original 1968 definition with the current protocol

misconceptions.claim: including more data points (the crown) always makes a summary index more accurate
misconceptions.provenance: pre-chapter prior contradicted by Tessaly's objection that the crown's cant 'records handling rather than building'

ideas.label: Tessaly's concord index (the current standard) excludes the crown
ideas.anchor: Since 1986 the Serrow survey protocol has used Tessaly's version of the index, which leaves the crown out

misconceptions.claim: the crown-excluded version is the older, superseded one
misconceptions.provenance: reverses which version is current; the text states Tessaly's crown-excluded version has been standard 'since 1986'

misconceptions.claim: the crown is excluded for the same reason the footing is (it follows the slope of the ground)
misconceptions.provenance: misapplies the footing's exclusion rationale to the crown, when the crown's actual reason is that passers reset it when turning the pell stone

ideas.label: a hob (a single reversed course flanked by agreeing ones) signals an upcoming junction, not noise
ideas.anchor: A hob does not give the route direction; it announces that a second route branches off before the next cairn

misconceptions.claim: a lower concord score always signals a less reliable or worse-built cairn
misconceptions.provenance: pre-chapter prior contradicted by 'A low concord is not always noise'

misconceptions.claim: a hob points the route in the reversed course's own direction
misconceptions.provenance: reverses the hob's actual function: it announces a branch ahead rather than giving direction itself

misconceptions.claim: a hob is the same thing as a randomly mis-canted or collapsed course
misconceptions.provenance: conflates a deliberately-placed hob with an accidental fault, which the text treats as a separate category strangers 'generally recognise as unreadable and ignore'

misconceptions.claim: in the worked example, the west-canted course three means the route turns west
misconceptions.provenance: misreads the worked example exactly as the text's own named error: 'A careless reading takes the west cant of course three as the message, because it is the odd one out'

ideas.label: the Marhaug pattern: concord helps strangers monotonically but locals read low-concord cairns slightly better
ideas.anchor: Local walkers show the reverse, which Tessaly named the Marhaug pattern after its first observer

misconceptions.claim: more internal agreement in a signal is always easier to read, for any reader
misconceptions.provenance: pre-chapter prior contradicted by locals reading low-concord cairns slightly better than high-concord ones

misconceptions.claim: it is strangers, not locals, who read low-concord cairns better, since they aren't anchored by expectations
misconceptions.provenance: reverses which population the Marhaug pattern describes

ideas.label: guild cairns (which use hobs) average lower concord than shepherds' cairns (which don't)
ideas.anchor: shepherds' cairns have a higher concord on average than guild cairns, as Marhaug had predicted
ideas.reason: sub-example of SC-10 (hob); the guild-vs-shepherd concord difference is a specific instance already covered by the broader hob idea, not an independent hold

ideas.label: the Tessaly effect: experienced readers facing a register conflict correctly follow the dorran sense over a stale pell stone
ideas.anchor: Local walkers facing such a cairn almost always went down to the ford anyway, following the dorran sense

misconceptions.claim: the freshest evidence (the pell stone) should always override an older, fixed message
misconceptions.provenance: pre-chapter prior contradicted by locals correctly following the dorran sense in 52 of 71 conflicting cases

misconceptions.claim: the Tessaly effect is the same thing as the Orne effect
misconceptions.provenance: text explicitly warns 'The Tessaly effect must not be confused with the Orne effect'

misconceptions.claim: the Tessaly effect describes strangers being misled by a single reversed course
misconceptions.provenance: imports the Orne-effect finding (about strangers and hobs) into this context, which the text specifically attributes to 'experienced readers' facing a register conflict

ideas.label: the Orne effect: strangers who meet a hob misread the reversed course as the route direction, regardless of whether the next cairn is visible
ideas.anchor: a stranger who meets a hob reads the reversed course as the route direction, and so turns the wrong way

misconceptions.claim: the Orne effect is the same thing as the Tessaly effect
misconceptions.provenance: text explicitly separates the two: 'The Tessaly effect concerns experienced readers... The Orne effect concerns strangers and the courses alone'

misconceptions.claim: a stranger would check their reading against the next visible cairn and self-correct
misconceptions.provenance: contradicted by 'Orne found it just as common where the next cairn was in view as where it was not'

misconceptions.claim: the Orne effect describes experienced locals misreading a hob, not strangers
misconceptions.provenance: reverses the subject population the text names

ideas.label: lisk-sense reliability is highest at moderate traffic, not monotonically increasing with traffic
ideas.anchor: Lisk sense is most reliable on routes of moderate traffic

misconceptions.claim: busier routes should have more reliable pell stones, since more people maintain them
misconceptions.provenance: pre-chapter prior contradicted by 'On the busiest routes the stone is turned by walkers who do not know the convention'

misconceptions.claim: pell stone weight, not traffic level, is what mainly determines reliability
misconceptions.provenance: conflates the earlier note that heavier stones 'the more faithful its record' with the separate, traffic-driven cause of staleness

misconceptions.claim: on quiet routes the stone is turned too often rather than too rarely
misconceptions.provenance: reverses the quiet-route failure mode, which the text describes as the stone going 'stale'

ideas.label: Marhaug's height-based readability prediction was empirically falsified
ideas.anchor: Tessaly found that strangers misread cairns at the same rate whatever their height

misconceptions.claim: a plausible design rationale from a named authority should hold up empirically
misconceptions.provenance: pre-chapter prior contradicted by Tessaly's finding overturning Marhaug's four-to-six-course prediction

misconceptions.claim: the falsified height effect and the real traffic effect are the same finding
misconceptions.provenance: conflates two separately-tested claims in the same subheading, one confirmed (traffic) and one not (height)

ideas.label: restoration trades informativeness for readability: a rebuilt cairn is easier to read but says less
ideas.anchor: A restored cairn is easier for a stranger to read, but it says less than the cairn it replaced

misconceptions.claim: faithful restoration should preserve or improve a marker's information
misconceptions.provenance: pre-chapter prior contradicted by conservators erasing any hob and resetting the pell stone to a default position

misconceptions.claim: a restored cairn is both easier to read and more informative
misconceptions.provenance: reverses the trade-off the text states: easier to read precisely because it says less

misconceptions.claim: the restored, upslope-set pell stone is simply broken or wrong
misconceptions.provenance: misreads the reset stone as a malfunction rather than as carrying a default ('low ford') reading until next turned by a passer

discrimination_pairs.conflation: I read the pell stone's position as telling me which way the route goes, same as the courses — and if a passer just turned the stone, I take that as the builder's message updating.
The whole cairn is leaning, so that must be pointing somewhere — I'll read the tilt as a direction signal the same way I'd read a canted course.
The concord index is just 'how much the courses agree' — I don't track which version counts the crown, so I count it whenever it happens to have a cant.
It's the 'misread the cairn and go the wrong way' thing — I can't remember if it's the one about strangers missing a junction or the one about locals ignoring a stale pell stone.

do_not_test.item: author/researcher names and publication years (Marhaug's 1968 monograph, Brannagh, Tessaly's 1983 survey and 1986 protocol change, Orne 1990)
do_not_test.why: researcher/date attribution, not an idea; the named effects (Tessaly effect, Orne effect, Marhaug pattern) are the ideas, the bibliographic details are not

do_not_test.item: the three-part anatomy of a cairn (footing, body courses, crown) and the pell stone as a physical object
do_not_test.why: structural vocabulary/enumeration; criterion 2 only, needed as background, not as a hold

do_not_test.item: pell stone weight/heaviness as a record-fidelity factor
do_not_test.why: sub-point best used as a distractor in the traffic-reliability question (SC-15), not its own idea

do_not_test.item: false pell stones placed on Hessle cairns by visitors
do_not_test.why: illustrates the SC-1/SC-2/SC-3 conflation in the wild; belongs in a distractor or explanation, not its own question

do_not_test.item: specific comparative misrouting-cause rankings in Sources of error (false pell stones vs. frost lean; drover re-canting vs. frost lean; sudden spates vs. stale stones)
do_not_test.why: single-survey magnitude comparisons; volatile and too close-margin to safely order into a key/distractor split

do_not_test.item: the hask cairn (bedded pell stone) as a distinct fault category
do_not_test.why: the text itself resolves this into 'the same fault' as a stale stone; testing the old taxonomy would contradict the text's own correction

do_not_test.item: exact concord fractions as arithmetic (e.g. 'two in four, or 0.5') outside the SC-8/SC-9 worked-example application
do_not_test.why: the worked-example concord figures already carry the section's one R11-style durable-figure load-bearing budget and must not be re-used as load-bearing elsewhere
